title: The Journey of the Murle People
subtitle: From the eastern lands remembered in Murle oral tradition through Boma and the Pibor basin, the long journey that shaped Murle identity and homeland.
author: Murle Connect Editorial Team

body.heading: HISTORY O MURLO
paragraphs: The history of the Murle people is also a history of movement. Across generations, Murle communities moved through different landscapes, adapted to changing environments, separated into different branches, and eventually established a homeland centred on the Boma highlands and the Pibor basin.

The earliest part of this journey is not preserved in a single written historical record. Much of it comes from Murle oral traditions recorded by researchers who worked with Murle elders. These traditions remember an ancestral place called Jen in the east and describe a long movement through the Omo region, toward Lake Turkana, Kapoeta, the Maruwa Hills, Boma and the Pibor country.

This journey should not be understood as one migration in which every Murle person travelled together at the same time. Oral histories describe movements of communities, ancestors and groups over long periods. Some people remained behind, some separated from larger groups, and some communities developed new identities. The history of the Murle is therefore a story of movement, separation, adaptation and the formation of a shared identity.

body.heading: The Wider Eastern African Background
paragraphs: The Murle are a Surmic-speaking people whose language belongs to the Didinga-Murle branch of the Surmic language family. Surmic languages are spoken mainly in southwestern Ethiopia and adjoining areas of South Sudan. Linguistic relationships provide important evidence for understanding the wider historical connections between the Murle and neighbouring Surmic-speaking peoples.

Language, however, cannot by itself provide a complete migration map. The development of peoples and languages takes place over long periods through movement, contact, separation and cultural exchange. For this reason, Murle migration traditions are studied together with linguistic research, anthropology, historical documents and other evidence.
The early history of the Murle therefore belongs to a much wider eastern African history in which communities moved through changing ecological zones and interacted with neighbouring peoples.

body.heading: Jen: The Eastern Homeland Remembered in Oral Tradition
paragraphs: When Jonathan Arensen recorded Murle migration traditions, elders commonly pointed toward the east when describing the origin of their people. They used the word Jen, which carries both geographical and symbolic meaning in Murle understanding.

Jen was associated with the east, the direction of the rising sun and the direction from which rains were understood to come. Elders also described the ancestral country associated with Jen as mountainous.

The importance of Jen is therefore greater than the name of a single modern location. In Murle oral tradition, it represents an ancestral direction and a remembered homeland from which earlier generations began their long movement.

Because the earliest part of this account comes primarily from oral tradition, it should not be presented as a precisely mapped historical event. Its importance lies in the memory preserved by Murle elders and in the way that memory connects present-day Murle identity to an eastern ancestral homeland.

body.heading: The Journey toward the Omo River
paragraphs: Murle migration traditions describe an early movement southward through the region of the Omo River. The Omo connects the highlands of southwestern Ethiopia with the lands farther south toward Lake Turkana.

The movement through this region would have brought earlier Murle communities into contact with other peoples living across eastern Africa. The region was never an empty landscape. Communities depended on livestock, agriculture, hunting, water sources and seasonal resources, and different groups interacted with one another in many ways.

The traditional account does not necessarily describe a single group travelling in one continuous line. Communities could divide, establish new settlements, remain behind, or move again later. This is an important point when interpreting the journey because migration over generations is different from a single organized migration.

body.heading: Lake Turkana
paragraphs: According to the migration traditions recorded from Murle elders, the journey eventually brought ancestral Murle groups toward the region of Lake Turkana.

Lake Turkana and its surrounding landscapes have long been an important crossroads in eastern Africa. Different communities lived around the lake and in the neighbouring territories, making the region a place of interaction between peoples with different languages, livelihoods and political traditions.

For the Murle migration tradition, Lake Turkana represents an important stage in the long movement away from the eastern ancestral homeland and toward the territories where later Murle communities became established.

The account should not be interpreted as proof that every present-day Murle ancestor passed through exactly the same route. Rather, it records a collective memory of movement through a broad eastern African landscape.

body.heading: From Lake Turkana toward Kapoeta
paragraphs: The traditional journey then continues northward and westward into the region around present-day Kapoeta. This area lies within the wider landscape connecting southeastern South Sudan with the territories toward the Ethiopian border and the eastern African highlands.

As communities moved through different environments, access to water, pasture, livestock, agricultural land and protection would have influenced where people could settle and how long they remained in particular places.

The Kapoeta stage is particularly important in Murle oral history because traditions associate this period with the separation of groups that later became distinct communities. These traditions preserve a memory of a time when populations that shared older relationships developed different identities and territories.

body.heading: The Separation of Related Communities
paragraphs: Murle oral histories and linguistic research preserve memories of historical relationships between the Murle and other Surmic-speaking communities in the region.

Traditional accounts describe groups separating during the long period of movement. Some became associated with the Didinga, others with the Boya or Longarim, and others with the Tennet. These communities later developed their own identities, territories and political histories.

The historical relationship between these peoples should not be reduced to a simple story in which one modern ethnic group suddenly became several others. Ethnic identities develop over long periods. Language change, marriage, settlement, political organization, migration and interaction with neighbouring populations can all contribute to the development of distinct communities.

Modern linguistic research supports relationships among several of these Surmic languages, while oral traditions provide additional memories about how communities understand their shared past. Together, these sources help researchers investigate the deeper history of the region.

body.heading: Disease, Livestock and Hardship
paragraphs: Murle migration traditions also remember periods of severe hardship. Accounts recorded by Arensen describe disease affecting people and livestock and causing serious losses.

For communities whose lives depended heavily on cattle, the loss of livestock could have consequences far beyond the loss of animals. Cattle provided food, wealth and social value and played an important role in marriage and community life.

Environmental pressure, disease, competition over resources and relations with neighbouring communities could therefore influence decisions about movement. Migration was not simply a search for new land. It could also be a response to survival.

body.heading: The Maruwa Hills
paragraphs: The migration traditions eventually place the Murle in the region of the Maruwa Hills. This became another important stage in the development of the communities that would later establish themselves in Boma and the Pibor lowlands.

According to the traditional account, the Murle population was no longer moving as one body. Different groups followed different paths, influenced in part by their circumstances and access to livestock.

One branch moved toward the Boma highlands, while another continued toward the Pibor river system. These movements became important in shaping the geographical pattern of Murle society that exists today.

body.heading: The Journey toward Boma
paragraphs: Boma became one of the major centres of Murle life. The Boma Plateau is a highland environment with different ecological conditions from the lowlands around Pibor.

Murle communities living in the Boma highlands developed livelihoods centred more heavily on cultivation and small livestock than the cattle-centred pastoralism associated with much of the lowland Murle population.

These ecological differences contributed to different ways of life, but they did not create two separate peoples. Research on Murle identity shows that highland and lowland communities understand themselves as belonging to one broader Murle identity, sharing language, social institutions and historical connections.
The Boma Murle therefore represent an important branch of the wider Murle population and an essential part of Murle history.

body.heading: The Journey toward Pibor
paragraphs: Another major branch of the Murle population became established in the lowlands around the Pibor river system. The Pibor basin became the centre of a predominantly agro-pastoral Murle way of life.

The rivers and seasonal plains of the region provided water, grazing and agricultural opportunities. Important waterways and landscapes associated with Murle communities include the Pibor, Lotilla, Veveno and Kengen river systems.

Lowland Murle communities traditionally moved with livestock according to seasonal conditions. This movement was not aimless wandering. It was an organized response to rainfall, pasture, water, cultivation, livestock needs and the changing environment.
Over generations, the Pibor basin became a central part of the Murle homeland and an important centre of Murle political, social and cultural life.

body.heading: Boma and Pibor: One People, Different Environments
paragraphs: The distinction between Boma and Pibor is important in understanding Murle history, but it should not be used to divide the Murle into separate peoples.

The highland Murle of Boma developed livelihoods adapted to the plateau and surrounding hills, while the lowland Murle developed a stronger pastoral and agro-pastoral economy around the rivers and plains.

Researchers have documented these ecological and livelihood differences while also emphasizing the shared Murle identity connecting the two communities. Murle people from Boma and Pibor belong to the same wider ethnic community and share important linguistic and social institutions.
The two environments therefore represent different branches of Murle life within one broader historical and cultural world.

body.heading: A Homeland Shared with Other Peoples
paragraphs: The establishment of Murle communities around Boma and Pibor did not occur in an empty territory. Other communities also lived in the wider region, including Dinka, Nuer, Anyuak and other neighbouring populations.
Relations between communities varied over time. They included trade, marriage, social contact, competition over resources, movement, alliances and conflict.

Historical accounts must therefore avoid presenting the Murle migration as a simple story of entering an empty land and taking it over. Different communities have their own histories of movement and settlement, and those histories sometimes overlap.
What can be established more clearly is that over generations the Murle developed a strong connection to the Boma and Pibor landscapes and established communities that remain there today.

body.heading: People Who Remained Behind
paragraphs: A long migration does not mean that every person moves together or reaches the same destination. Murle oral histories and related research indicate that some people remained behind during different stages of movement.
Others may have married into neighbouring communities or become incorporated into different populations while retaining memories, names, languages or cultural connections from earlier generations.
This helps explain why the historical connections between Murle and neighbouring Surmic-speaking communities cannot always be understood through present-day ethnic boundaries alone.
The movement of the Murle therefore created not only new settlements but also networks of historical and cultural relationships extending beyond the communities that identify as Murle today.

body.heading: From Migration to Homeland
paragraphs: Over many generations, the movement of Murle communities gradually developed into a stronger attachment to particular territories.

Boma became a major highland centre. Pibor and the surrounding river plains became a major lowland centre. Families developed permanent or semi-permanent settlements while continuing seasonal movement where their livelihoods required it.
The landscape became more than a place where people lived. Rivers, hills, grazing areas, agricultural fields, cattle camps and settlements became part of collective memory and identity.

The long journey had therefore entered a new stage. The Murle were no longer simply communities moving through different territories. They had established a homeland in which generations could live, raise families, maintain social institutions and preserve cultural knowledge.

body.heading: The Murle before Colonial Rule
paragraphs: European colonial administration reached the region after Murle communities had already established their own social and political systems. Colonial rule did not create Murle society or the Murle homeland.

Before effective colonial administration, Murle communities organized their lives through kinship, clans, age-sets, customary authority, cattle ownership, settlement patterns and relationships between communities.

The arrival of colonial government introduced a different political system. Administrators began defining territories, appointing officials, recording populations and regulating relations between communities.

The colonial period therefore marked another major stage in the Murle journey: the transformation from living within locally organized territories to living within an externally imposed administrative state.

body.heading: Colonial Administration and Pibor
paragraphs: British administration gradually extended its authority over the southeastern Sudan region. Historical accounts describe the Murle as one of the communities whose effective incorporation into colonial administration occurred relatively late.

Colonial rule changed how territory and movement were understood. Seasonal movements that had previously been governed primarily by local customs, environmental conditions and relationships between communities increasingly took place within administrative boundaries.
Pibor later became an important administrative centre. Government institutions, schools, missions and new forms of communication gradually connected Murle communities to a wider political system.

These changes did not immediately erase traditional Murle institutions. Instead, customary authority and new government structures existed alongside one another, creating a new political environment for Murle society.

body.heading: The Twentieth Century and Civil Wars
paragraphs: The twentieth century brought major political upheavals to the region. Sudan became independent in 1956, but conflict between the central government and southern movements continued for decades.

The southern civil wars affected Murle communities deeply. Armed groups moved through Murle territory, civilians were displaced, political alliances changed, and communities faced difficult decisions about security and survival.

During different periods of the Sudanese civil wars, Murle communities were not politically uniform. Some Murle joined or supported southern movements, while others formed relationships with or fought alongside forces supported by the Sudanese government.
These divisions should be understood in the context of the wars and the security pressures facing communities rather than as evidence that the Murle ceased to share a common identity.

body.heading: The Journey into South Sudan
paragraphs: The creation of an independent South Sudan in 2011 marked another major political stage in Murle history.

Much of the Murle homeland became part of the new Republic of South Sudan. The region later known as the Greater Pibor Administrative Area became a major administrative framework for Murle communities, while Murle communities also remained across the international border in southwestern Ethiopia.

The international border created a new political division across a region whose communities had historical connections that predated modern states. Yet language, family relationships, cultural practices and memories continued to connect Murle communities across borders.
The political map had changed, but the deeper historical connections of the people had not disappeared.

body.heading: The Murle Journey Today
paragraphs: The Murle journey did not end with settlement in Boma and Pibor. Movement remains an important part of Murle life.

Lowland communities continue to organize many aspects of pastoral life around seasonal conditions, while highland communities maintain agricultural livelihoods adapted to the Boma environment. People also move for education, employment, trade, family responsibilities, security and other opportunities.
Murle communities now exist not only in villages and cattle camps but also in towns such as Pibor and Boma, in other parts of South Sudan, in Ethiopia and within the wider diaspora.

Modern movement is therefore different from the migrations remembered in oral tradition, but both involve adaptation to changing circumstances. The Murle continue to carry language, family connections, cultural knowledge and historical memory with them wherever they live.

body.heading: The Meaning of the Journey
paragraphs: The Murle migration tradition is not simply a list of places. It is a story about how a people understand their connection to the land and to previous generations.

The journey remembered by Murle elders begins in the east, in the ancestral direction associated with Jen. It continues through the Omo region and toward Lake Turkana, then toward Kapoeta and the surrounding country. Communities separate, move through different environments and eventually establish themselves in Boma and the Pibor basin.
Along the way, the people experienced hardship, environmental change, disease, interaction with neighbouring communities and changes in their livelihoods.

The journey also explains why Murle history cannot be understood only through modern administrative boundaries. The history is older than South Sudan, older than Sudan and older than the borders separating South Sudan from Ethiopia.

body.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: The history of the Murle is a history of movement, survival, adaptation and settlement. From the eastern homeland remembered as Jen, through the Omo and Lake Turkana regions, across the Kapoeta area and the Maruwa Hills, generations of movement eventually connected the Murle with the Boma highlands and the Pibor basin.

The people who reached Boma and Pibor did not become two different peoples. They developed different livelihoods because they lived in different environments, but they continued to share a wider Murle identity, language and social connections.

The journey also produced relationships with neighbouring communities. Some people remained behind, some communities separated and developed their own identities, and others continued toward the lands that became the Murle homeland.

Today, Boma and Pibor remain central to Murle identity. The highlands and lowlands represent different environments and ways of life, but together they form an important part of the historical landscape of the Murle people.

The journey of the Murle is therefore more than a story about where the people travelled. It is the story of how generations of people carried their language, memories, relationships and identity across changing landscapes until those movements became the homeland remembered today.
The journey continues. New generations of Murle are moving through a changing world while carrying the history of those who came before them.

historicalNote: This article combines Murle oral migration traditions with linguistic, anthropological and historical research. The account of Jen, the Omo River, Lake Turkana, Kapoeta, the Maruwa Hills and the movement toward Boma and Pibor is primarily preserved through oral traditions recorded by researchers, including Jonathan Arensen. The sequence should therefore be understood as a historical tradition rather than as a fully verified modern migration map. Relationships between Murle, Didinga, Boya or Longarim, and Tennet communities are also complex and should not be reduced to a single migration event.
